title: Leave Me Today, Khawla, or Lower Your Eyes
intro: The long recension gives these words to Tarafa ibn al-Abd after the king's letter has delivered him to his death. The speaker tells Khawla how to mourn him, recalls what he has done for his people, then calls the king to account for the letter he carried. Ali al-Jundi prints sixty verses and records early disagreement over their authorship. Abu Ali al-Qali transmits a substantial group of the verses on generosity and Abdal's counsel as a poem delivered by al-Hakam ibn Abdal before the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj.

translation: Leave me today, Khawla, or lower your eyes.
A humped calamity has fastened its bite.
1.sharh: He gives Khawla the choice of leaving or looking away from his distress. Calamity has taken animal shape, its humped back and relentless bite visible before he tells us what has happened.

translation: It has shaken my heart from its resting place,
and today my wing has no strength to rise.
2.sharh: His heart has been dislodged and the wing that might carry him out of danger hangs useless. His predicament has deprived him of inner steadiness and of freedom to act.

translation: I used to bear life's losses stoutly.
I could live among men even when I disliked them.
3.sharh: He once bore repeated losses and could rub along with men he disliked. The unusual image of “wearing” men conveys the closeness and friction of dealing with them.

translation: I am sweet to a friend,
bitter to men of rancour, showing them my hate.
4.sharh: Sweetness and bitterness are what the other person tastes in dealing with him. A friend knows the first, an enemy who nurses a grudge the second.

translation: I grow rich without being spoiled by wealth.
I offer what I can to anyone who asks a loan.
5.sharh: He measures good fortune by what it frees him to give. The word for a loan also prepares for the poem's repeated reckoning of what one person owes another.

translation: At times I fall into the tightest straits,
then regain the ease of wealth with my honour intact.
6.sharh: Poverty can tighten around him and then let him go. The achievement he claims is to emerge with both a livelihood and a good name.

translation: I rescue my kinsman from trouble once
his foot slips like a camel on treacherous ground.
7.sharh: Aid arrives after the fall, when a mere warning would be useless. A camel losing its footing makes the weight of a relative's predicament palpable.

translation: I give him my wealth, my honour and my help,
though his ribs be folded round hatred of me.
8.sharh: A kinsman's breast can close over hatred of him. He still puts his resources, reputation and active support at that man's disposal.

translation: My forbearance covers him, though I could make him feel
the flesh-stripping consequences of bitter words.
9.sharh: Words could flay the offender. He makes that power plain so the listener can tell how much protection his silence has afforded.

translation: Until my trouble lifted and the sky cleared, no trusted friend
reached me with a loan or a grant.
10.sharh: He waited out the crisis without borrowing from a friend or receiving a portion set aside for him. The clearing weather marks the end of a need he had to bear alone.

translation: It was God's bounty, my own calling,
and the tightening of the camel's breast-girth.
11.sharh: The need to earn a living takes concrete shape in the straps of a riding camel. He had to saddle up and go in search of what he needed.

translation: I value myself too highly to be seen cringing
before a patron who gives little and wrings out sweat.
12.sharh: The smallness of the gift makes the supplicant's ordeal more pointed. He would have to sweat for the dubious privilege of owing such a patron.

translation: I keep harm from my family as a point of honour,
though I repay anyone who cuts me off in kind.
13.sharh: He protects his family, yet he answers a breach of ties with a breach. The words recall a loan repaid in kind. Al-Jundi identifies estrangement as the particular injury returned here.

translation: I offer kindness and my disposition stays clear
when even men of pure character grow clouded.
14.sharh: Good temper is easy while things go well. He claims his remains like clear water even when circumstances cloud the dispositions of otherwise sound men.

translation: I carry my undertakings through with firm resolve
when other affairs can scarcely move an inch.
15.sharh: He gives his concerns a direction and follows them to their end. Against his forward motion stands the near standstill of business in difficult times.

translation: I give judgement against myself when a claim reaches me.
Some men receive judgements and never deliver one.
16.sharh: He will act as judge even when he is the losing party. Others settle what they owe only when somebody else has pronounced against them.

translation: I have forbearance, yet my anger,
when people rouse me, serves to guard my honour.
17.sharh: His temper has a particular use. Although ready to let an injury pass, he draws on anger where his good name needs defending.

translation: If they seek my friendship, I turn kindly towards them.
There is no good in one who never returns to gentleness.
18.sharh: The people who provoked him can also end the quarrel. He counts the ability to soften again among the virtues of someone capable of anger.

translation: Many an objector to what was right I made change his plea,
telling him, “The verdict is not as you give it.”
19.sharh: An opponent has tried to pass off his own case as a judgement. Brief, direct speech puts him back in the position of a claimant.

translation: I took him through terrors until I left him
in a tight place, unable to stir or proceed.
20.sharh: The encounter ends in a place with no room for manoeuvre. That confinement also describes what has happened to the opponent's argument.

translation: I wear no two colours with the people I know.
Miserliness, know this, belongs to neither my sky nor my earth.
21.sharh: Two colours would mean two faces shown to the same person. Heaven and earth then give the denial of meanness the widest imaginable bounds.

translation: I have carried out this part of Abdal's counsel,
and as Abdal instructed, so I shall act.
22.sharh: Abdal's name makes the virtues just listed a charge handed down. In al-Qali's transmission under al-Hakam ibn Abdal, the second half explicitly names the counsellor as the speaker's father.

translation: When I die, weep for what I truly was,
and urge the mourning women on with all your might.
23.sharh: His address to Khawla returns with instructions for the future. The catalogue of deeds has supplied the mourners with the material for an honest lament.

translation: If I perish, do not rank me with a weakling,
a man of unravelling cord and slackened twist.
24.sharh: Resolve is a well-twisted rope. A man with no staying power comes apart strand by strand, and that is the comparison he asks Khawla to refuse.

translation: I swear by the Lord of the camels dancing towards Mina,
racing one another on the days of rites and departure,
25.sharh: The camels' rapid gait looks like dancing. Naming the divine Lord of these pilgrim mounts gives weight to the assertions about fear and honour that follow.

translation: if I feared men whose offences lay plain before me
for dread of a broad-chested, biting disputant,
26.sharh: The clause hangs on “if”. He grants the possibility of fear for a moment so he can answer it with the remembered conduct of men who have already tested him.

translation: long have they shaken my spear and rallied against me,
yet my shaft never softened in the bite.
27.sharh: His spear is both a weapon and the measure of his firmness. Opponents have handled it roughly for years without finding a soft point.

translation: They know how intent I am on charging them,
and how often I overlook their rancour.
28.sharh: The clansmen have seen him ready to charge them, yet he often lets their hostility pass. Al-Jundi understands the running as a rush to battle, which prepares for the gallop to protect his kin in the next verse.

translation: I guard what my clan must defend,
and my gallop shields those I gallop out in front of.
29.sharh: His protection takes the form of riding out in front. Repeating the gallop in verb and noun makes the horse's movement stand between his people and danger.

translation: When action comes, I am neither slack nor powerless,
but bold, striking men whichever way they come.
30.sharh: His strength is measured at the moment of encounter. He represents himself plunging into the press without first picking out an easy opponent.

translation: After the sons of Dhara ibn Abdal have been taken away,
who expects the pleasure of a life at ease?
31.sharh: The departure of a named family breaks the run of boasts. If those men could be taken away, his own expectations of comfort suddenly look precarious.

translation: They passed. We stayed, hoping for life after them.
Everyone who stays follows the one who goes.
32.sharh: “Stays” and “goes” seem at first to describe opposite fates. The survivor is simply further back on the same track.

translation: Enough for me, the sickness that will not leave me
and the grief of troubles that scarcely lets up.
33.sharh: The general reflection narrows back to his own body. An illness that stays and grief that barely lets him go keep him pinned in the present.

translation: Do you see how my eye has poured out its tears
until the lid can scarcely close?
34.sharh: His eye supplies evidence anyone can see. So much water has run from it that it can scarcely do the simple work of closing its lid.

translation: As if the pungent juice of fresh spikenard were in both eyes,
scattered by the winds through leaves of saltbush.
35.sharh: The tears sting as well as flow. He imagines plant juice carried on the wind, a physical comparison for the heat grief has put in both eyes.

translation: As water-seekers look upon swift horses
in fetters, gathering at saddlecloth and girth.
36.sharh: Al-Jundi reads the fast horses, fettered among pack gear, as an image of a noble creature put to the wrong use. They give the poet a figure for his own captivity.

translation: Take care, people of al-Mushaqqar and al-Safa,
cousins of ours. We pay a debt in kind.
37.sharh: He names the places and claims kinship in the same breath as his warning. The old language of lending now carries the possibility of retaliation.

translation: You two, tell Bakr ibn Wa'il in Iraq
of a cup the Nasrid gave its drinker, burning hot.
38.sharh: The conventional pair of messengers is to carry home a bitter experience. A king of the house of Nasr plays the host, but the cup he offers burns.

translation: If al-Nu'man kills my people,
it is the first death, the prelude to their seizure.
39.sharh: The long version names al-Nu'man here, alongside a tradition centred on Amr ibn Hind. The immediate danger is figured as the first instalment of a collective death.

translation: Then bear down on al-Nu'man in battle
and on Ka'b ibn Zayd. Keep him from his fresh milk.
40.sharh: The contrast is between going to battle and being at leisure to drink milk. The men blamed for the speaker's fate are to be shaken out of the comforts of home.

translation: They brought me to death deliberately and sent out
horses tireless in the gallop to work their treachery.
41.sharh: He accuses the pair of intent. The horses' unflagging speed gives the betrayal the force of a decision already being carried out.

translation: I perished. Caution saved the man of Yashkur.
He swerved as a camel swerves from slippery ground.
42.sharh: The traditional companion is al-Mutalammis, who took precautions over his letter. The camel image returns, this time with an animal alert enough to avoid the place where it could slip.

translation: Had I feared treachery in giving obedience,
Banu Malik would have fought off the one who ruled.
43.sharh: Here “religion” has the older sense of obedience. His clan could have challenged the order, had he suspected what his compliance was helping to bring about.

translation: How strange the palm trunk they raise me on,
and crucifixion my share from foes and all I have given.
44.sharh: The trunk is the timber on which he sees himself being raised. “My loan” calls back his earlier reckoning of services repaid, now with a cruel return.

translation: We used to stand in strength among our people,
Duba'a, long accustomed to striking men from every side.
45.sharh: The name Duba'a identifies the people whose former strength he invokes. His solitary exposure on the trunk is measured against what it once meant to stand among them.

translation: Abu Mundhir, you have destroyed so many. Spare some of us.
Mercy upon mercy. Some evils are easier than others.
46.sharh: The doubled form of “mercy” asks for compassion again and again. His plea is modest in its terrible arithmetic. Even now the king can choose a lesser evil.

translation: Abu Mundhir, if it is war with us you want,
our dwelling is open and its approaches wide.
47.sharh: He offers the king a place where an encounter could be open. The breadth of the land is a rebuke to the narrow means by which he himself has been trapped.

translation: Abu Mundhir, who will meet the armoured fighters
when horses wheel among broken spears?
48.sharh: He invites the king to picture a moment when a champion is needed. The broken shafts on the field bear witness to the work the condemned man could have done.

translation: Abu Mundhir, my letter was a lure.
I did not yield my wealth or honour to you willingly.
49.sharh: Trust made him the carrier of his own sentence. To carry it was never to consent to everything the letter put at the king's disposal.

translation: Abu Mundhir, who has strength for the troubles you see,
that drive established ways towards undoing?
50.sharh: Established courses are being driven towards reversal. From the treachery over one letter he turns to what becomes of public obligations when their keeper fails.

translation: Abu Mundhir, you aimed at keeping faith, then shrank from it.
You shied away as a camel shies from slippery ground.
51.sharh: The same wary sidestep that saved the man of Yashkur now shames the king. What the king avoids, as though it were a dangerous patch of ground, is keeping his word.

translation: You see people in crowds at his door,
each living man waiting to learn what he refuses or allows.
52.sharh: At court a crowd waits on decisions that can take effect with a word. The scene makes the reach of his present authority visible before the speaker challenges it.

translation: You are no crowned ruler over all the living,
nor over the dead in the hollows of the earth.
53.sharh: He imagines the king's realm stretched from the surface of the earth down to its graves. Naming the dead is enough to expose a limit to any living king's rule.

translation: They say, “May you refuse the curse”, though the curse is his lot.
Soon, you who refuse good, you will be known for bringing low.
54.sharh: A royal greeting wishes the king free of any deed deserving a curse. Changing “curse” to “good” turns the compliment against him. On the reading heard here his reputation will be for bringing people low.

translation: I swore beside the sacred stones that I would perish
in a fatal waste, with neither delight nor ease.
55.sharh: The standing stones give the oath a sacred setting. He foresees the loss of his life in a place offering none of the ordinary comforts men hope to find.

translation: Mighty Taghlib will come raiding you at dawn.
No breadth of land will save you from the host.
56.sharh: Taghlib arrives with the dawn. Two senses of the rhyme word can be heard here, open space and a great army. The breadth of the first is no shelter from the second.

translation: And people in al-Mushaqqar and al-Safa will be clothed
in showers of death pouring down without respite.
57.sharh: Death becomes both a garment thrown over the towns and a downpour falling in successive bursts. The warning sent to the two settlements has become a picture of their fate.

translation: Taghlib turns on the man of Abd al-Qays at his border,
and cuts Ka'b ibn Sahl off from his fresh milk.
58.sharh: Taghlib's raid reaches the governor even on his own ground. Fresh milk recalls the earlier threat to Ka'b ibn Zayd. This verse names Ka'b ibn Sahl.

translation: I lend no counsel to the obstinate kinsman
who will not turn to me or speak his mind.
59.sharh: Generosity too has conditions. A counsellor cannot reach a relative who neither leans towards him nor lets him know what is on his mind.

translation: Not every cheat can hurt you with his deceit,
nor can you please everyone you wish to honour.
60.sharh: Malice can miss and goodwill can fail to please. The two halves allow other people less power over the outcome, and the speaker less control over theirs.

1.1.4.head: خَولَة
1.1.4.meaning: Khawla, the woman addressed here and asked later to lead the mourning.

1.1.6.meaning: Lower your gaze, turn your eyes away from me.

1.2.3.head: حَدباء
1.2.3.meaning: Humpbacked. The calamity takes the shape of a she-camel with its teeth fast in him.

2.2.2.head: جَناح
2.2.2.meaning: A wing, here the strength that once lifted him.

2.2.6.head: نَهض
2.2.6.meaning: The power to rise or take flight.

3.1.6.head: مُرَزَّأ
3.1.6.meaning: Repeatedly struck by loss or bereavement.

3.2.3-4.head: لَبّاس الرِّجال
3.2.3-4.meaning: “One who wears men”, someone accustomed to keeping company even with difficult people.

3.2.6.head: بُغض
3.2.6.meaning: My dislike of the people I keep company with. Both long editions speak of dislike without the first-person pronoun.

4.1.4.head: إِنَّ
4.1.4.meaning: “And I, for my part”. He repeats the assertion as he turns from friend to enemy. Both long editions shorten the second wa-innani to wa-inni.

5.1.4.head: بَطِرَ
5.1.4.meaning: Become arrogant or heedless in prosperity.

5.2.2.head: مَيسور
5.2.2.meaning: Whatever part of his means he can make available.

6.2.5.head: عِرض
6.2.5.meaning: Honour, the good name a person can keep through hardship.

7.1.2.meaning: A kinsman or ally with a claim on his protection.

7.2.6.head: الدَّحض
7.2.6.meaning: Slippery ground where even a camel loses its footing.

8.2.3-4.head: مَحنِيّ الضُّلوع
8.2.3-4.meaning: “With ribs bent round it”, nursing a hatred he keeps inside.

9.2.2.head: بَرى
9.2.2.meaning: Shave or whittle away, here the action of hurtful words on flesh.

10.1.4-5.head: تَجَلّى وأَسفَرَ
10.1.4-5.meaning: “Lifted and grew light”, of trouble passing like darkness at dawn.

10.2.6.head: فَرض
10.2.6.meaning: An allotted gift, set beside a loan that must be repaid.

11.2.2.head: حَيازيم
11.2.2.meaning: The breast and the parts of the animal's chest encircled by its harness.

11.2.4.head: الغَرض
11.2.4.meaning: The girth that secures a camel's saddle round its breast.

12.2.1-2.head: ذو مِنَّة
12.2.1-2.meaning: A benefactor whose gift makes the recipient feel beholden.

12.2.6.head: الرَّحض
12.2.6.meaning: Sweat drawn by embarrassment or effort.

13.2.4.head: المُقارِض
13.2.4.meaning: Someone who breaks off relations. Al-Jundi explains that the speaker answers the breach in kind.

14.1.4.head: خَليقَة
14.1.4.meaning: Disposition, the habitual temper in which he treats others.

14.2.6.head: مَحض
14.2.6.meaning: Pure, of unblemished character or descent.

15.1.2.head: هَمّ
15.1.2.meaning: Undertakings that occupy him and that he means to carry through.

15.1.3.head: الزَّماع
15.1.3.meaning: A settled resolution to go through with something.

16.1.1-3.head: قَضى عَلى نَفسِهِ
16.1.1-3.meaning: “Give judgement against myself”, acknowledge another person's right even at one's own expense.

16.1.6.head: نابَ
16.1.6.meaning: Befell me, came to my door.

17.2.2.head: هَزَّ
17.2.2.meaning: Shook or roused me, here provoked me to anger.

19.1.1.head: مُعتَرِض
19.1.1.meaning: A disputant who stands in the way of a rightful claim.

20.2.2.head: ضَنك
20.2.2.meaning: Cramped, painfully constricting, of the corner into which an opponent is driven.

20.2.4.head: أَكَدَّ
20.2.4.meaning: Exert himself to force a way out.

21.1.2-3.head: ذو لَونَين
21.1.2-3.meaning: “Of two colours”, two-faced in one's dealings.

21.2.5.head: سَماء
21.2.5.meaning: His sky, paired with his earth to encompass everything that belongs to him.

22.1.6.head: عَبدَل
22.1.6.meaning: Abdal, named in the counsel. In al-Qali's account al-Hakam ibn Abdal calls him “my father”.

23.2.1.head: حُضّي
23.2.1.meaning: Urge on, addressed to Khawla as she gathers the mourners.

23.2.4-5.head: مَدى الحَضّ
23.2.4-5.meaning: “To the furthest reach of urging”, as earnestly as you can.

24.1.2.head: عَدَلَ
24.1.2.meaning: Put me on a level with another man.

24.2.4.head: المَريرَة
24.2.4.meaning: A firmly twisted rope, an image for strength of purpose.

24.2.5.head: النَّقض
24.2.5.meaning: Unravelling a twist, undoing the very thing that gives a rope strength.

25.1.3.head: الرّاقِصات
25.1.3.meaning: The “dancers”, camels whose quick gait gives the appearance of dancing.

25.1.5.head: مِنى
25.1.5.meaning: Mina, a stage of the pilgrimage near Mecca.

25.2.3.head: المَشاعِر
25.2.3.meaning: The sacred sites at which the pilgrimage rites take place.

26.2.5.head: جَدَل
26.2.5.meaning: Contention, especially skill and tenacity in argument.

27.1.4.head: قَناة
27.1.4.meaning: A spear shaft, the measure of his resilience.

27.1.5.head: أَجلَبَ
27.1.5.meaning: Raised a clamour and rallied others against him.

28.1.4.head: شَجِيّ
28.1.4.meaning: Preoccupied, with his mind set on something. Al-Jundi takes his concern here to be the prospect of fighting.

28.1.5.head: عَدو
28.1.5.meaning: Running, here charging the men he addresses, in al-Jundi’s explanation.

28.2.6.head: أَغضى
28.2.6.meaning: Close the eyes, hence overlook an injury.

29.1.3.head: ذِمار
29.1.3.meaning: People, property and honour that one is bound to defend.

29.2.3.head: رَكَضَ
29.2.3.meaning: Spurred a mount into a gallop, here to intercept danger.

30.2.2.head: مُدِلّ
30.2.2.meaning: Bold through confidence in his own strength.

30.2.5-6.head: عَن عُرض
30.2.5-6.meaning: “From whatever side”, without picking out an opponent.

31.1.2-5.head: بَنو ذَرى اِبنِ عَبدَل
31.1.2-5.meaning: Banu Dhara ibn Abdal, the kinsmen whose loss prompts the question.

32.2.6.head: إِثر
32.2.6.meaning: A footprint or trail left by someone who has gone ahead.

33.1.6.head: بارِح
33.1.6.meaning: Departing from me, of an illness that will not go away.

33.2.5.head: وَجد
33.2.5.meaning: The intensity of the grief these troubles cause.

33.2.6.head: أَفضى
33.2.6.meaning: Passes away or comes to an end, in al-Jundi’s gloss. His grief scarcely lets up.

34.1.6.head: سِجام
34.1.6.meaning: Tears running in an unbroken flow.

34.2.7.head: أَغضى
34.2.7.meaning: Lower the eyelid until it covers the eye.

35.1.2.head: مُجاج
35.1.2.meaning: Liquid pressed or drawn out of something.

35.1.4.head: الوَرث
35.1.4.meaning: Fresh, here of the spikenard. Both long editions have warth with final th, which al-Jundi glosses as “fresh”. One of his manuscripts reads ward, with a final d.

35.2.3.head: الأَرواح
35.2.3.meaning: Winds, the agents that scatter the plant juice.

35.2.6.head: الحِمض
35.2.6.meaning: Salt or sour-tasting desert herbage browsed by camels.

36.1.2.head: نَظَرَ
36.1.2.meaning: Looks at the horses. The two continuous transcripts and the caption have ينذر, which the isolated clip renders as yandhuru, “vows”. Both diwan editions use the verb for looking.

36.1.3.head: الوُرّاد
36.1.3.meaning: People coming down to a watering place.

36.2.2.head: نَدا
36.2.2.meaning: Gather or draw close to the place named.

36.2.4.head: الحِلس
36.2.4.meaning: The saddlecloth laid directly against an animal's back.

37.1.4.head: المُشَقَّر
37.1.4.meaning: Al-Mushaqqar, a stronghold at Hajar in the historical region of Bahrayn.

37.1.5.head: الصَّفا
37.1.5.meaning: Al-Safa, a site paired with al-Mushaqqar in eastern Arabia. Al-Jundi identifies it here as a watercourse.

37.2.4.head: جَزى
37.2.4.meaning: We repay it in kind. Al-Nahari speaks for his own people. Both long editions address the people warned, “you repay it”.

38.1.3-4.head: بَكر العِراق
38.1.3-4.meaning: Bakr of Iraq, the Iraqi branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il to whom the two messengers are sent.

38.2.3.head: النَّصرِيّ
38.2.3.meaning: Al-Nasri, a king of the house of Nasr at al-Hira.

38.2.5.head: رَمَض
38.2.5.meaning: Scorching heat, here the burn felt by the drinker.

39.1.3.head: النُّعمان
39.1.3.meaning: Al-Nu'man, the king named in this recension of the story.

39.2.4.head: تَقدِمَة
39.2.4.meaning: A first instalment or foretaste of what follows.

40.2.1-3.head: كَعب بن زَيد
40.2.1-3.meaning: Ka'b ibn Zayd, named alongside al-Nu'man as a target of retaliation.

41.1.2.head: أَورَدَ
41.1.2.meaning: Led me to a watering place, here the place of death.

41.1.5.head: جَرَّدَ
41.1.5.meaning: Sent out horses stripped and ready for a raid.

42.1.1.head: رَدِيَ
42.1.1.meaning: I came to ruin or perished.

42.1.3.head: اليَشكُرِيّ
42.1.3.meaning: Al-Yashkuri, a man of Yashkur identified in the commentary with al-Mutalammis, who escaped the danger of his letter.

43.1.4.head: الفَتك
43.1.4.meaning: A surprise attack on a man who has trusted his assailant.

43.1.6.head: الدّين
43.1.6.meaning: Obedience or allegiance to the ruler.

43.2.1-2.head: بَنو مالِك
43.2.1-2.meaning: Banu Malik, the kinsmen the speaker counts on for protection.

44.1.3.head: الجِذع
44.1.3.meaning: The trunk of a palm used as the timber of execution.

44.2.4.head: عُداة
44.2.4.meaning: Foes, people who act against him.

45.1.3-4.head: ذو مِرَّة
45.1.3-4.meaning: A person of strength and firm resolve.

45.2.1.head: ضُبَيعَة
45.2.1.meaning: Duba'a, the branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il to which Tarafa belonged.

45.2.2.meaning: From long ago, of an established practice.

46.1.1-2.head: أَبو مُنذِر
46.1.1-2.meaning: Abu Mundhir, the king's byname. Tradition uses it for Amr ibn Hind in Tarafa's story. This poem also names al-Nu'man.

46.2.1.head: حَنانَيك
46.2.1.meaning: “Mercy twice over”, a plea for repeated mercy.

47.2.4.head: مُفضٍ
47.2.4.meaning: Open and accessible, of country that an enemy can cross to reach them.

48.1.4.head: الكُماة
48.1.4.meaning: Armoured fighting men, warriors covered by their weapons.

48.2.7.head: رَفض
48.2.7.meaning: Scattered or broken pieces of spear shafts.

49.1.4.head: غَرور
49.1.4.meaning: A deception that lulls someone into trusting the instrument of his destruction.

49.1.5.head: صَحيفَة
49.1.5.meaning: The letter he carried to the governor, containing the order for his death in the traditional account.

50.2.3.head: حَدا
50.2.3.meaning: Drive onwards, as a camel driver urges his animals on with song.

50.2.4.head: الشَّرائِع
50.2.4.meaning: Established ways or courses, literally paths leading down to water.

51.1.3.head: رامَ
51.1.3.meaning: Aimed at, sought to do something.

51.2.1.head: حادَ
51.2.1.meaning: Swerved aside, abandoned the course you had begun.

52.2.3-6.head: رَدَّ وأَمضى
52.2.3-6.meaning: “What he sends back and what he puts through”, the ruler's refusals and grants.

53.1.5.head: مُمَلَّك
53.1.5.meaning: Installed as king, invested with power.

53.2.5-6.head: نُكتَة الأَرض
53.2.5-6.meaning: “A hollow in the earth”, evoking the place of burial.

54.1.2-3.head: أَبَيتَ اللَّعن
54.1.2-3.meaning: “May you refuse the curse”, a royal greeting wishing the ruler free of deeds that would bring a curse on him.

54.2.5.head: الخَفض
54.2.5.meaning: Bringing low or abasing. The recording and Seligsohn have khafd. Al-Jundi reads habd, which he glosses as injustice and treachery.

55.1.3.head: النُّصُب
55.1.3.meaning: Sacred standing stones at which rites were performed and oaths sworn.

55.2.1.head: مَتلَفَة
55.2.1.meaning: A place or waste in which a traveller can perish.

55.2.3.head: غَبط
55.2.3.meaning: A happy condition that others might envy.

56.1.2.head: الغَلباء
56.1.2.meaning: Al-Ghalba', “the mighty”, an epithet of the tribe Taghlib.

56.1.3.head: تَغلِب
56.1.3.meaning: Taghlib ibn Wa'il, the tribe whose impending raid the speaker foretells.

56.2.4.head: عَرض
56.2.4.meaning: Breadth or open space. The repeated word can also designate a great body of troops.

57.2.3.head: اِستَهَلَّ
57.2.3.meaning: Come pouring down, as a heavy shower begins.

58.1.3.head: العَبدِيّ
58.1.3.meaning: Al-Abdi, a man of the tribe Abd al-Qays.

58.2.1-3.head: كَعب بن سَهل
58.2.1-3.meaning: Ka'b ibn Sahl, the name in this performance and the appendix recension. Al-Jundi's main text names Awf ibn Amr.

58.2.4.head: اِختَرَمَ
58.2.4.meaning: Snatch him away or cut his life short.

59.1.2.head: رَفَدَ
59.1.2.meaning: Lend assistance, here by offering advice.

59.2.7.head: أَفاضَ
59.2.7.meaning: Open up in conversation and speak freely.

60.2.5.head: كَرامَة
60.2.5.meaning: The honour one wishes to show another person.
